proposal.root_problem: Refund-status support tickets are driven by refunds failing during processing in payment-db due to invalid IBAN format (5 of 5 sampled refunds show status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, E-01), not by slow support response, since agents already reply within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h across 900 tickets, E-02). Customers perceive endless waiting because the underlying refund never completes, which the requester misattributes as a response-speed problem (E-03, contradicted by E-01/E-02).
proposal.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers get instant answers about refund status (initial request from SH-SUP, CL-01), premised on the belief that support reply speed is the bottleneck.
symptoms: Customers report waiting indefinitely for answers about refund status (CL-01/CL-02, E-03)
Refund-status support tickets persist despite support agents replying within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h, E-02)
Sampled refund records in payment-db show FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT rather than completing (E-01)
causal_chain: Customer submits a refund request whose IBAN fails payment-db validation, producing status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01).
Because this processing step fails, the refund never completes and no resolving status reaches the customer.
The customer, seeing no completed refund, opens or follows up on a support ticket asking about refund status.
Support agents reply within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h across 900 tickets, E-02) but cannot resolve the ticket because the defect is in payment-db processing, not in agent responsiveness.
The customer continues to experience the refund as stuck and reports 'waiting forever', which the requester reframes as a response-speed issue (E-03) despite E-01/E-02 contradicting that framing.

assumptions.statement: The 5-record payment-db sample in E-01 is assumed representative of the broader refund failure rate rather than an unusual small subset.

Refund-status tickets measured in ticket-db (E-02) are assumed to substantially be the same population affected by the IBAN failures in payment-db (E-01); no direct join evidence links specific tickets to specific failed refunds.
IBAN format failures are assumed to stem from a data-validation defect in the refund pipeline rather than from isolated, uncorrectable customer input errors.

key_points: The original request (CL-01, from stakeholder SH-SUP) was to build a chatbot because 'customers wait forever' for refund-status answers, framing the issue as slow support response (CL-02, E-03).

Investigation found this framing is contradicted: ticket-db shows 900 tickets with a median 2.0h response time against a 24h SLA, i.e. support is well within SLA (E-02/F-02), rejecting H-SLOW-SUPPORT-RESPONSE.

Instead, payment-db shows 5 of 5 sampled refund records FAILED with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01/F-01), supporting H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE: refunds are failing to process due to an IBAN validation defect in the refund pipeline (P-REF), and customers are asking about refunds that never actually complete.

The problem definition (PD-1) was revised accordingly: the root problem is a payment-pipeline validation defect, not a response-speed issue; this passed the DEFINE gate as CONDITIONAL_PASS with the deferred item VOB-U-FAILURE-SCALE.

What was released: the refund-pipeline defect assessment deliverable for P-REF (work item W-WI-DEFECT-ASSESSMENT, status DONE), documenting the IBAN-format validation defect as the supported root cause, using the already-run payment-db data (E-01).

The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION: the defect assessment is released, but production use is conditioned on the open limitations listed below, and no fix, scale-up query, or stuck-refund remediation was performed in this session.

A dependency check against bank-api (to resolve whether the IBAN defect depends on bank-api's settlement_status integration, VOB-R-2/U-BANK-API-DEPENDENCY) could not run because the bank-api tool is UNAVAILABLE/DEGRADED with ACCESS_DENIED and no fallback path; this was logged as a HOLD (not a transient failure).
Several candidate hypotheses (H-REFUND-PROCESSING-BACKLOG, H-SUPPORT-LACKS-REFUND-VISIBIL, H-TICKET-VOLUME-SURGE) remain unresolved candidates and were not confirmed or ruled out.
limitations_explained: DEFINE Gate result was CONDITIONAL_PASS, not a full pass: the critical unknown U-FAILURE-SCALE was deferred into VOB-U-FAILURE-SCALE rather than resolved.

VOB-U-FAILURE-SCALE (HIGH impact, required before release) is still OPEN: it asks what proportion of all refund-status tickets, beyond the 5-record sample, are due to IBAN failures versus other causes; its blocking scope (quantify_iban_failure_impact, correlate_tickets_with_failures) is outside this release's scope.

VOB-R-2 (required before production) is still OPEN: whether the IBAN defect is purely a payment-db logic issue or also depends on the bank-api settlement_status integration is unresolved, because that check could not be run.
The bank-api tool is UNAVAILABLE/DEGRADED (ACCESS_DENIED), with no fallback path, so U-BANK-API-DEPENDENCY and VOB-R-2 could not be investigated in this session.

The IBAN-failure baseline (5 of 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, E-01) rests on a 5-record sample from payment-db whose completeness is UNKNOWN (per A-SAMPLE-REPRESENTATIVENESS and U-SAMPLE-SIZE-VALIDITY), so the true population-wide failure rate is not established.

There is no join key linking specific support tickets to specific failed refunds (A-TICKET-FAILURE-LINKAGE), so the correlation between IBAN failures and ticket volume remains inferential even if the sample is scaled up; M-TICKET-IBAN-CORRELATION has no current value.

The actual remedy -- having payments engineering fix the IBAN validation logic in P-REF -- was not performed; it was identified as a remedy (SR-FIX-IBAN-VALIDATION-DEFECT) but marked not feasible in contest time.
The already-stuck refunds R-0 through R-4 (observed FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT in E-01) still require remediation outside this session, since no write or deploy tool was available to correct them.
proposal.summary: The stakeholder SH-SUP initially requested a chatbot (CL-01/CL-02) believing customers wait too long because support is slow. Evidence contradicted this: ticket-db shows support replies within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h, E-02), while payment-db shows 5 of 5 sampled refunds FAILED with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-01), supporting the hypothesis that an IBAN-format validation defect in the refund pipeline (P-REF) is the real root cause, not response speed (H-SLOW-SUPPORT-RESPONSE was REJECTED; H-IBAN-FORMAT-FAILURE was SUPPORTED). The problem definition was reframed around this defect and passed the DEFINE gate as CONDITIONAL_PASS. The deliverable released is the refund-pipeline defect assessment for P-REF, documenting the IBAN-format defect as root cause, with decision RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION. The release carries this label because a required pre-production verification (whether the defect depends on the bank-api settlement_status integration, VOB-R-2) could not be completed -- the bank-api tool is UNAVAILABLE/ACCESS_DENIED with no fallback -- and a required pre-release scale verification (VOB-U-FAILURE-SCALE) remains open outside this release's scope. No actual fix, scale-up query, or remediation of stuck refunds was performed.
